title: IS COMMUNION REALLY THE BODY AND BLOOD OF JESUS—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT HAPPENS AT THE LORD’S TABLE?
paragraphs: IS COMMUNION REALLY THE BODY AND BLOOD OF JESUS—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT HAPPENS AT THE LORD’S TABLE?
Symbolic, spiritual, or literally Christ Himself? The shocking words of Jesus, the warning that made the Corinthian church tremble, and the sacred truth we cannot afford to treat casually.
There is something deeply unsettling about the night Jesus broke the bread.
He knew who would betray Him.
He knew who would deny Him.
He knew His disciples would scatter when the darkness came.
And He knew that before another day had passed, His body would be wounded, His blood would be shed, and the very people He came to save would watch Him die.
Yet in those final hours, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He took bread.
He gave thanks.
He broke it.
And then He spoke words that Christians have been wrestling with for nearly two thousand years.
“This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.” — Luke 22:19 (KJV)
Then He took the cup.
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.” — Luke 22:20 (KJV)
Not merely, “Think about Me.”
Not simply, “Remember that I was a good teacher.”
He spoke of His body. His blood. His sacrifice.
And what He commanded that night became one of Christianity's most sacred practices.
But here is the question that still divides sincere, Bible-believing Christians:
When we receive Communion, are we simply eating bread and drinking wine as symbols? Are we encountering Christ spiritually? Or do the bread and wine truly become His body and blood?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question follows.
What if we have spent so much time arguing about what is happening to the bread that we have forgotten what Jesus intended to happen in our hearts?
Before you answer, stay with me.
Because the Scriptures contain a warning about Communion that should make every Christian examine the way they approach the Lord's Table.
And they also contain a promise of grace that no struggling sinner should overlook.
Imagine yourself in that upper room.
The air is heavy. The disciples do not fully understand what is coming. The Teacher they have followed, loved, and trusted is speaking about betrayal, suffering, and departure.
Then Jesus takes ordinary bread and gives it extraordinary significance.
The Greek text of Luke 22:19 records His words:
Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον.
Touto estin to sōma mou to hyper hymōn didomenon.
“This is my body, which is given for you.”
Notice the phrase ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν (hyper hymōn).
It means “for you” or “on your behalf.”
Those two words carry the weight of the Gospel.
Jesus was not merely announcing that suffering was approaching.
He was identifying His coming death as a sacrifice given on behalf of others.
For the disciples who would fail Him.
For Peter, who would deny knowing Him.
For the fearful followers who would abandon Him.
And for sinners like us, who desperately need the mercy of God.
This is where Communion begins.
Not with a debate about religious terminology.
Not with a contest over which Christian tradition has the most convincing explanation.
It begins with Jesus Christ giving Himself for sinners.
But we must not pretend that the theological question is unimportant.
It matters because Jesus' words matter.
And faithful Christians have reached different conclusions precisely because they take those words seriously.
Some understand Communion primarily as a memorial ordinance.
Others believe Christ is truly present and received spiritually by faith.
Still others confess that the consecrated bread and wine are truly His body and blood, although they explain that mystery in different ways.
These are not trivial differences.
They concern the meaning of Christ's words, the nature of His presence, and the way His people participate in the sacred meal.
So what does Scripture actually say?
We must begin by allowing each passage to speak in its own context.
In Luke 22:19, Jesus commands:
“This do in remembrance of me.”
The Greek word translated “remembrance” is ἀνάμνησις (anamnēsis).
It refers to remembrance or recollection.
But we should not automatically reduce biblical remembrance to a passing mental thought.
Jesus established this meal in the context of Passover, when Israel remembered God's mighty deliverance from slavery in Egypt.
In Exodus 12, the Passover meal was closely connected to God's saving action and His covenant relationship with His people.
The Hebrew word זִכָּרוֹן (zikkārôn) means “memorial” or “remembrance.”
The connection is significant, although the Hebrew and Greek words do not by themselves settle every question about the nature of Christ's presence in Communion.
Biblical remembrance can involve much more than recalling historical information.
It can involve worship, thanksgiving, covenant identity, and the proclamation of God's saving works.
And now Jesus stands before His disciples as the fulfillment toward which the Passover story points.
The lambs of Israel's ancient deliverance anticipated a greater redemption.
Paul later writes:
At the Lord's Table, believers remember not merely that a man died, but that the Son of God willingly gave Himself for their salvation.
Yet does remembering Christ mean that the bread and cup are only symbols?
That conclusion cannot be established from the word anamnēsis alone.
A memorial can be profoundly meaningful without requiring a change in the substance of the elements.
But remembrance also does not automatically exclude a real participation in Christ.
The word itself does not resolve the entire debate.
And this is where we need to be careful.
Because the moment we make one Greek word carry more theological weight than it can bear, we risk confusing our interpretation with the authority of Scripture itself.
Now consider something even more startling.
Long before the Last Supper, Jesus spoke words that caused some of His listeners to recoil.
In John 6:53, He declared:
“Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.” (KJV)
Imagine hearing those words as a first-century Jewish listener.
The Law of Moses strictly prohibited consuming blood.
Leviticus 17:11 explained that the life of the flesh is in the blood and connected blood with atonement.
The Hebrew word דָּם (dam) means “blood.”
Against that biblical background, Jesus' language would have sounded astonishing.
Eat His flesh?
Drink His blood?
What could He possibly mean?
Jesus continued:
“Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.” — John 6:54 (KJV)
Then came another extraordinary statement:
“For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.” — John 6:55 (KJV)
The Greek reads:
ἡ γὰρ σάρξ μου ἀληθής ἐστιν βρῶσις, καὶ τὸ αἷμά μου ἀληθής ἐστιν πόσις.
Hē gar sarx mou alēthēs estin brōsis, kai to haima mou alēthēs estin posis.
The expression ἀληθής (alēthēs) means “true” or “genuine.”
Jesus was speaking about something of ultimate spiritual reality.
But we must ask what He meant by eating and drinking.
Was He speaking directly about the future Lord's Supper?
Was He using vivid language to describe believing in Him and receiving the saving benefits of His death?
Or does the passage illuminate both faith in Christ and sacramental participation in Him?
Christians disagree.
And the context deserves careful attention.
Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus said:
“He that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.” — John 6:35 (KJV)
Notice the parallel.
Coming to Jesus answers hunger.
Believing in Jesus answers thirst.
That is a major reason many Protestant interpreters understand eating His flesh and drinking His blood as powerful imagery for receiving Christ through faith.
John 6:47 also declares that the one who believes in Christ has everlasting life.
This interpretation takes seriously the chapter's repeated emphasis on faith.
But Christians who understand John 6 eucharistically point to the increasingly explicit language of flesh, blood, eating, drinking, and abiding in Christ.
They argue that these words reach beyond a purely mental act of remembrance and illuminate the mystery of Communion.
Both approaches must reckon with the whole passage.
And both must acknowledge something essential.
Jesus is not teaching that salvation comes through a physical act detached from faith in Him.
His entire discourse centers on Himself as the bread of life, the One sent from heaven, the One who gives life to the world.
Later, in John 6:63, He says:
“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.” (KJV)
This does not mean that His incarnation or sacrificial flesh is worthless. That would contradict His earlier declaration that He gives His flesh for the life of the world.
Rather, His words warn us against understanding His teaching in merely fleshly, unaided human terms.
Life comes through the Spirit.
And the saving work of Christ must be received according to the truth He reveals.
John 6 does not explicitly narrate the institution of the Lord's Supper.
That historical and literary fact matters.
The discourse certainly has profound connections with the themes Christians celebrate in Communion, but whether it directly teaches a particular doctrine of Eucharistic presence remains debated.
We should not erase that distinction merely because one interpretation feels emotionally compelling.
Scripture deserves more than our strongest feelings.
It deserves our careful attention.
But now we come to a passage that should disturb anyone who thinks Communion can be treated as an empty religious routine.
The apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians about the Lord's Supper.
And he was not congratulating them.
Their gatherings had become marked by division, selfishness, humiliation, and disregard for poorer believers.
Some were eating while others went hungry.
Some were drinking excessively while others were left with nothing.
They had turned a meal meant to proclaim Christ's self-giving love into an occasion for displaying their own lack of love.
And Paul confronted them.
He reminded them of the words Jesus spoke on the night He was betrayed.
Then he declared:
“For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.” — 1 Corinthians 11:26 (KJV)
Do not miss that.
Communion looks backward to the cross.
It looks inward toward the condition of our hearts.
It looks outward toward the unity of Christ's people.
And it looks forward to His return.
Every time the church faithfully observes the Lord's Supper, it announces that Jesus died, that His sacrifice matters, and that the crucified Savior is coming again.
But Paul does not stop there.
He writes:
Then:
“But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.” — 1 Corinthians 11:28 (KJV)
And finally:
“For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.” — 1 Corinthians 11:29 (KJV)
The KJV's word “damnation” here translates κρίμα (krima), which means “judgment.”
In this context, Paul is warning about divine judgment or discipline, not declaring that every unworthy participant is automatically condemned eternally.
That distinction is crucial.
Because someone reading this right now may be carrying a terrible memory.
Perhaps you took Communion while secretly struggling with sin.
Perhaps you received the bread and cup while your marriage was collapsing.
Perhaps you were sitting in church with a smile on your face while bitterness was eating away at your heart.
Perhaps you knew you had been living a double life.
And now you are wondering whether God rejected you at the table.
Listen carefully.
Paul does not say that only sinless people may receive Communion.
If sinless perfection were required, no ordinary believer could approach.
The warning concerns receiving in an unworthy manner.
The Greek word ἀναξίως (anaxiōs) means “unworthily” or “in an unworthy manner.”
It describes the manner of participation, not a requirement that the participant must have achieved personal moral perfection.
That does not make the warning less serious.
It makes the invitation to honest repentance all the more urgent.
Paul calls believers to examine themselves.
Not to perform religious self-hatred.
Not to pretend they have never sinned.
But to recognize the holiness of the Lord, the significance of His sacrifice, and the responsibilities of belonging to His body.
The Corinthian problem was not merely that individuals had private moral failures.
They were dishonoring one another at the very meal that proclaimed the self-giving love of Jesus.

When Paul warns about failing to discern the body, interpreters differ over whether he refers primarily to Christ's body represented or received in the Supper, to the gathered church as Christ's body, or to both.
The immediate context of selfish treatment toward fellow believers gives the communal dimension particular force.
And Paul's earlier words in 1 Corinthians 10:16–17 are essential here.
He asks:
“The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” — 1 Corinthians 10:16 (KJV)
The Greek word translated “communion” is κοινωνία (koinōnia).
It means participation, fellowship, or sharing.
Paul uses the same word concerning the cup and the blood of Christ.
Then he explains that believers, though many, are one body because they share in the one bread.
This language is deeper than casual remembrance.
Yet it does not, by itself, define exactly how Christ is present or whether the bread and wine undergo an ontological change.
It establishes that the Lord's Supper is a holy participation bound to Christ and His people.
And that truth should change how we approach it.
You cannot sincerely celebrate the sacrifice of a Savior who laid down His life for others while deliberately despising the brothers and sisters He purchased with His blood.
You cannot boast about the cup of the new covenant while refusing to confront the cruelty, pride, or division you are nurturing.
You cannot treat the table as a spiritual performance while your heart remains defiantly closed to repentance.
Communion is not an excuse to remain unchanged.
It is a summons to remember the One whose grace calls us into a transformed life.
And now we must face the question directly.
Is Communion symbolic, spiritual, or literally the body and blood of Christ?
The answer depends in part on what we mean by those words.
A symbol is not necessarily empty.
A spiritual reality is not necessarily imaginary.
And a real presence does not necessarily mean a crude, physical interpretation in which Christ's body is eaten as ordinary flesh.

Roman Catholic theology teaches transubstantiation: that through consecration the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood, while their sensory appearances remain. This is not a claim that the elements visibly turn into human flesh and blood.

Eastern Orthodox Christians also confess the true body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, while generally emphasizing the sacred mystery rather than defining the change through the same scholastic explanation.
Lutheran Christians confess Christ's true body and blood as genuinely given and received with the bread and wine, while rejecting transubstantiation as their explanation.
Reformed Christians traditionally affirm that believers truly partake of Christ spiritually through the Holy Spirit and faith, without teaching that the bread and wine change substance.

Many Baptist, evangelical, and other Protestant churches understand the bread and cup principally as memorial signs that proclaim Christ's finished sacrifice and call believers to faith, obedience, gratitude, and unity.

These descriptions do not capture every nuance within each tradition, but they show why the disagreement cannot honestly be reduced to “Christians who believe the Bible” versus “Christians who do not.”
The disagreement is about how to interpret and integrate biblical passages that all these traditions regard as sacred.
And we should not falsely claim that the original Greek settles every doctrinal dispute.
It does not.
The phrase “This is my body” is powerful, but the Greek verb ἐστιν (estin), meaning “is,” does not independently prove either a literal change of substance or a purely symbolic meaning.
Context and theological interpretation remain necessary.
Likewise, the biblical language of participation does not automatically establish transubstantiation, and the command to remember does not automatically establish memorialism.
Faithfulness requires us to distinguish what Scripture explicitly states from the theological conclusions Christians draw from it.
Still, beneath these disagreements, certain truths shine unmistakably.
Jesus instituted the Supper.
He connected the bread and cup to His body and blood.
He commanded His followers to remember Him.
Paul taught that believers proclaim the Lord's death through it.
Paul also taught that participation is a serious matter involving fellowship with Christ and responsibility toward His people.

And the New Testament consistently teaches that salvation rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith, not upon the supposed power of a religious performance to save apart from Him.
Ephesians 2:8–9 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
Hebrews 10:10 declares that believers are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
The cross is not an unfinished transaction waiting for human beings to complete it.
Jesus cried:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30 (KJV)
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It means “it has been finished” or “it has been accomplished.”
In John's Gospel, this declaration marks the completion of the work Jesus had come to fulfill.
We should not reduce it to a slogan about financial debt, as though that alone exhausts its meaning.
Its significance is greater.
The crucified Son has accomplished His mission.
The Lamb of God has given Himself.
The sacrifice upon which our salvation depends has been offered.
And no faithful understanding of Communion should diminish the sufficiency of that sacrifice.
Whether Christians understand the Supper as sacramental participation, spiritual communion, or memorial proclamation, the meal must direct worship toward Christ rather than toward human achievement.
Because bread cannot replace the Savior.
A cup cannot substitute for repentance.
And religious familiarity cannot manufacture a living relationship with God.
Consider Judas.
He spent years close to Jesus.
He heard the sermons.
He witnessed the miracles.
He belonged outwardly to the circle of disciples.
Yet his heart was moving toward betrayal.
The Gospels place Judas within the events surrounding Jesus' final meal, although Christians differ about the precise chronology of his departure and participation in the institution of Communion.
We should therefore avoid claiming more than the narratives clearly establish.
But the spiritual warning remains.
It is possible to be physically close to sacred things while remaining spiritually resistant to the Savior they reveal.
That should concern us.
Not because we must live terrified that every weakness means we have lost God's love.
But because outward religion can become a hiding place for inward rebellion.
You can know the words of the liturgy and still refuse to forgive.
You can understand the theological debates and still neglect the poor.
You can defend the Lord's Table passionately and still mistreat people who bear the Lord's name.
And you can receive Communion week after week while quietly refusing to surrender the sin that is destroying your life.
The question is not merely whether you can explain the bread.
The question is whether you are willing to listen to the Christ who broke it.
And here is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Not from the people at church. You have learned how to appear fine in front of them.
You know when to stand.
You know when to bow your head.
You know how to say “Amen.”
But God knows the conversation you deleted.
He knows the resentment you keep feeding.
He knows the promises you made and quietly abandoned.
He knows the secret habit you keep defending.
He knows the wounds that have made trusting anyone difficult.
And He knows the shame that follows you into the sanctuary.
You may feel as though the table exposes everything you have tried to conceal.
In one sense, it does.
It reminds us that sin is serious enough that the Son of God gave His life for our redemption.
But it also reminds us of something we desperately need to hear.
The cross does not merely expose the depth of our sin. It reveals the greater depth of God's mercy toward sinners who come to Christ.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He declared that he was ready to suffer.
Then, under pressure, he denied Jesus three times.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The crushing memory of his own confidence.
The unbearable knowledge that he had denied the One he loved.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and commissioned him to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21.
That is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter for a repentant disciple.
And perhaps that is the truth someone needs today.
You may have failed Him.
You may have wandered.
You may have spent months or years wearing a Christian identity while your heart drifted farther from obedience.
But the answer is not to pretend that nothing happened.
The answer is to return to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Seek reconciliation where you have caused harm.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
And trust the Savior whose mercy is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears earn salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Now picture the Lord's Table again.
The bread is broken.
The cup is offered.
The words of Jesus are remembered.
And somewhere in the congregation sits a man who has spent the week struggling with anger.
A woman who is exhausted from carrying grief nobody sees.
A young believer who keeps falling into the same temptation and wonders whether genuine change is possible.
A father who regrets the words he spoke to his children.
A daughter who is learning how to forgive without pretending that the harm she suffered was acceptable.
A person who has not prayed sincerely in months.
Their stories are different.
Their wounds are different.
Their responsibilities are different.
But they share one desperate need.
Jesus Christ.
The Lord's Supper is not a stage on which Christians display their superiority.
It is a holy proclamation of the Savior upon whom Christians depend.

This does not mean every person should participate without regard to faith, repentance, baptism, or the discipline of their church. Christian traditions differ on admission to Communion, and believers should approach it with respect for Scripture and the faithful guidance of their congregation.
But it does mean that the central message of the table is not human perfection.
It is Christ's saving sacrifice.
And that changes everything.
Because the same Jesus who said, “This is my body,” also said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28, KJV).
The same Jesus who spoke of His blood also prayed for those who crucified Him.
The same Jesus who warned about judgment also welcomed repentant sinners.
His holiness is real.
His warnings are real.
And His grace is real.
We do not honor Him by weakening any of these truths.
So perhaps the most faithful way to approach the Lord's Table is with both reverence and gratitude.
Reverence, because the death of Jesus is not ordinary.
Gratitude, because His sacrifice was given for those who could never save themselves.
Humility, because we must never confuse our theological understanding with personal holiness.
Love, because the body of Christ is not a collection of religious competitors but a people called to serve one another.
And faith, because our hope rests not in our flawless performance but in the crucified and risen Lord.
If you belong to a church that teaches Christ's real sacramental presence, receive its teaching seriously and seek to understand how it honors the words of Jesus.
If you belong to a church that emphasizes spiritual participation, remember that the Spirit's work is neither imaginary nor insignificant.
If your church understands Communion primarily as a memorial, do not allow the word “symbol” to become an excuse for casualness or spiritual indifference.
A memorial of the crucifixion of the Son of God should never become meaningless routine.
And wherever you worship, remember Paul's warning.
Examine yourself.
Discern the body.
Reject selfishness.
Seek unity without sacrificing truth.
Remember the cross.
Proclaim His death.
Await His coming.
And above all, look to Jesus.
Because Communion was never meant to make the church forget the Gospel while arguing over the elements.
It was instituted by the Savior who is Himself the heart of the Gospel.
The bread directs us to His body given for us.
The cup directs us to His blood of the new covenant.
The meal calls us to remember His death and live in the light of His resurrection and promised return.
And no matter how thoroughly we study the mystery, we must never lose sight of the Person.
The greatest tragedy would not be leaving the table without winning an argument. It would be leaving the table without taking seriously the Christ to whom it points.
So here is a question worth asking before your next Communion service.
Not simply, “What does my denomination teach?”
That is an important question, and it deserves thoughtful study.
But ask something deeper as well.
“Lord Jesus, what in my life have I refused to surrender to You?”
Perhaps it is pride.
Perhaps it is bitterness.
Perhaps it is a secret sin.
Perhaps it is the belief that your past is too shameful for God's mercy.
Perhaps it is the assumption that because you attend church, you no longer need to examine your heart.
Whatever it is, bring it into the light.
Do not bargain with Jesus.
Do not try to purchase His acceptance through religious performance.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because His sacrifice is sufficient.
His resurrection is real.
And His grace is not exhausted by the failures of those who turn back to Him.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
The scandal is not merely that sinners have sinned.
It is that the holy Son of God willingly entered our broken world, endured the cross, and gave Himself for the redemption of the undeserving.
The grace is that those who repent and trust in Him can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
And the transformation is that His mercy does not leave us content to remain as we were.
It calls us to follow Him.
To love what He loves.
To turn away from what destroys us.
To care for His people.
And to proclaim His Gospel until He comes.
Take a moment to pray.

You can also share what your church teaches about Communion, together with the Scripture that shapes your understanding. Let the conversation be marked by biblical conviction, charity, and a willingness to listen.
Someone reading the comments may be carrying a burden that your testimony helps them bring before the Lord.
Not to pressure them.
Not to embarrass them.
But to remind them that Jesus Christ came to call sinners to repentance.
There is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical resources accessible to people who want to grow deeper in their relationship with Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to encourage serious Bible study, spiritual growth, and a deeper understanding of the Gospel.
And maintaining, developing, and expanding this work requires time, effort, and resources.

You may choose to view it as part of your personal generosity toward Christian ministry, but it should not be confused with a biblically required tithe or with an offering owed to God. Scripture teaches generous, willing giving—not giving under compulsion.
As Paul writes:
These products are simply another way to carry messages of faith, encouragement, and biblical truth into everyday life.
A thoughtful share may help this message reach someone who has never seriously considered the meaning of Christ's sacrifice.
We would be grateful to walk with you as we continue learning Scripture, confronting difficult questions, encouraging repentance, and pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
But never forget this.
The goal is not to build a following around a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And that brings us back to the upper room.
Back to the broken bread.
Back to the cup.
Back to the words that have echoed through centuries of Christian worship.
“This is my body.”
“This cup is the new testament in my blood.”
“Do this in remembrance of me.”
The disciples did not yet understand the full horror of what awaited Him.
But Jesus knew.
He knew about the nails.
He knew about the cross.
He knew about the grave.
And still, He gave thanks.
He broke the bread.
He offered the cup.
And He gave Himself.
So the next time you approach the Lord's Table, do not allow familiarity to steal your reverence.
Do not allow theological disagreement to make you careless with Scripture or cruel toward fellow believers.
Do not allow shame to convince you that sincere repentance is pointless.
And do not allow the outward act of Communion to replace the inward necessity of trusting and following Jesus Christ.
The table directs our attention to a sacrifice no sinner could earn.
A covenant established through the blood of Christ.
A Savior who died and rose again.
And a promise that His people will proclaim His death until He comes.
You may spend a lifetime trying to understand everything about the bread and the cup—but never forget the Savior who gave Himself for you.
